newsitem.title: INDIA: India skyscraper blaze prompts new safety measures.
newsitem.headline: India skyscraper blaze prompts new safety measures.

text.p: City officials on Thursday vowed to tighten fire safety procedures in India's commercial capital after three people died in a blaze that raged for three hours in an office tower block.

The fire, which gutted three floors in the 25-storey Express Towers, home to one of India's premier newspaper houses as well as several major Indian and multinational firms, has prompted officials to survey fire precautions in the area.
The cause of the fire is not yet known.

The skyscraper is located in the prestigious Nariman Point business district, where office space is among the world's most expensive, thanks to a combination of archaic rent laws and land use regulations.
"Everybody wants to use every inch of space," said Shridhar Joshi, a senior city official.

"There are so many wooden partitions and little cubicles," he added. "There's no ventilation, and if a fire breaks out you can only go to the lift or the staircase. There is no space to do anything else."
Officials said as many as 35 skyscrapers spread over an 80-acre (0.8-hectare) area in the heart of the business district, were at risk of similar fires, as well as many other buildings.
Joshi told Reuters the government of Maharashtra state, where Bombay is located, had drafted tough new legislation to ensure that fire precautions were followed.
"The bill is being considered by the federal government," Joshi added. "It will prescribe the enforcement machinery and the penal provisions applicable."
In the meantime the administration plans to warn the owners of Bombay high-rises of the fire hazards they face, he said.
Joshi said some skyscraper owners planned to put in fire escapes on the outside of the buildings, in addition to the sprinkler and hosepipe systems many already have.
"But that's not so good from the security point of view," Joshi said. "Many owners think thieves could easily use them to get in and loot the offices."
Ironically, the tower block in which Wednesday's fire took place, is one of the best-equipped to fight fires, owner Vivek Goenka said.
"When it was built, fires were kept in mind," Goenka, also managing editor of the Indian Express group, said.

"It's built only of concrete, stone and glass. No wood was used. It's the only multi-storeyed building with small balconies on the outside. People can escape the blaze inside, and come out and wait to be rescued."
But the tallest ladder the Bombay Fire Brigade possesses can go only upto 60 metres, or as high as the 3th floor, officials said, limiting the rescue option.
"These are probably the longest in the world," said deputy fire chief officer M.G. Sirkhot. "We do the best we can."
